title: Async-First Team Norms
body:
Async-first team norms are the shared agreement that most team communication happens in writing, on a schedule the reader controls, rather than by interrupting whoever is available right now. A team working async-first still meets, but meetings are reserved for decisions that genuinely need everyone in the same conversation at the same time. Everything else goes into a written update, a shared document, or a tracked task, where it can be read, answered, and found again later. The norm protects focused work, gives quieter teammates an equal chance to contribute, and leaves a readable record of what was decided and why.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part async norm. First, the team names which channels are for urgent interruption and which are for ordinary written updates, so nobody has to guess whether a message needs an instant reply. Second, every request states what is needed, by when, and what happens if nobody answers, so a reader can act without a follow-up meeting. Third, decisions are written down where the work lives, with the options considered and the reason for the choice, not left in chat history. Fourth, the team agrees response windows, such as within one working day for ordinary requests, instead of expecting instant replies. Fifth, a weekly review checks whether the norms are holding or whether meetings are creeping back in for things writing could have handled.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for async-first team norms. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: sync-needed: 2 ['budget sign-off', 'outage alert']; async-handled: 3 ['weekly status', 'design review', 'holiday cover'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a team is interrupted constantly, when teammates work different hours, or when decisions keep getting relitigated because nobody can find where they were made. Do not use it as an excuse to avoid hard conversations, because disagreements about direction, performance, or conflict still deserve a live conversation. Do not use it where genuine urgency exists, such as an outage or a safety issue, where immediate contact is the right tool. title: Shared Document Discipline
body:
Shared document discipline is the set of habits that keeps a team's shared documents findable, current, and trustworthy. Without it, a team ends up with five copies of the same plan, nobody sure which one is current, and new joiners reading outdated instructions. With it, every document has one home, one owner, a clear title, and a visible date, so anyone can tell at a glance whether they are reading the live version. The discipline is boring on purpose: it trades a little upfront tidiness for a large saving in confusion later.

Method. The working method for this record is a six-rule document discipline. First, one document per topic lives in one agreed place, and copies elsewhere link back to it instead of duplicating it. Second, the title says what the document is and who it is for, without clever abbreviations. Third, the owner is named on the document and is responsible for keeping it current. Fourth, the date of the last real update is visible, so staleness is obvious. Fifth, changes that matter are summarized at the top, so readers do not have to diff the whole document. Sixth, archived documents are marked archived and moved out of the live folders, so search results stop surfacing dead plans.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for shared document discipline. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record when a team shares plans, guides, or reference material that more than one person edits or reads. Do not use it as a substitute for version control on code or legal documents, where formal tooling is the right choice. Do not use it to justify deleting history, because archived versions are still useful when a decision needs to be explained later. title: Handoff Checklists
body:
A handoff checklist is the short written list that passes a piece of work from one person to another without dropping anything. Handoffs fail in predictable ways: the receiver does not know what is done, what is still open, what is blocked, or who to ask. A good checklist answers all four before the handoff conversation starts, so the conversation can focus on judgment calls instead of status archaeology. The checklist is especially valuable when someone goes on leave, changes teams, or hands a task to a colleague in another time zone.

Method. The working method for this record is a seven-item handoff checklist. First, the work's current state is stated in one paragraph, including what is finished and what is not. Second, open items are listed with their next action and their owner. Third, blockers are named with what would unblock them. Fourth, key contacts and where to find them are listed. Fifth, passwords, access, and permissions are transferred through proper channels, never pasted into the checklist itself. Sixth, deadlines and commitments already made are listed so the receiver does not accidentally break them. Seventh, the receiver confirms understanding in writing, and the handoff is only complete when that confirmation exists.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for handoff checklists. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: complete: 5 of 7; missing: ['blockers', 'receiver confirmation'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any transfer of responsibility, from a day's absence to a permanent role change. Do not use it as a replacement for the handoff conversation on complex work, because the checklist prepares the conversation rather than replacing it. Do not use it to hand off work that is undocumented chaos, because the checklist will expose the gaps, which is useful, but the gaps still need filling. title: Decision Logs
body:
A decision log is a running record of the decisions a team has made, each entry stating the decision, the date, the people involved, the options considered, and the reason for the choice. Teams without one relitigate the same questions every few months, because the reasoning left with whoever was in the room. Teams with one can answer a newcomer's why did we do it this way by pointing at an entry instead of reconstructing a debate from memory. The log does not need to be long: one short paragraph per decision is enough, written at the time the decision is made.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-field decision entry. First, the decision itself is stated plainly, so a reader knows what was settled. Second, the date and the decider or deciding group are recorded. Third, the options considered are listed briefly, including the option that was rejected, so the log shows the choice was real. Fourth, the reason for the choice is written in ordinary language, including any trade-off accepted. Fifth, the entry notes what would cause the decision to be revisited, so the team knows when new information should reopen it. Entries are kept in one place, in date order, and linked from the work they affect.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for decision logs. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: matches for 'release': [('2026-09-15', 'Weekly release on Fridays')] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for decisions that will outlive the meeting where they were made, such as tool choices, scope calls, and policy settings. Do not use it for trivial choices that nobody will ever revisit, because logging everything buries the decisions that matter. Do not use it as a weapon in blame discussions, because a log written for accountability after the fact stops being an honest record. title: Responsibility Mapping
body:
Responsibility mapping is the practice of writing down, for each piece of work, who does it, who is accountable for it, who should be consulted, and who should be informed. The best-known shape for this is the RACI pattern, where each task gets one accountable person, at least one responsible person, and named consulted and informed people. The point is not the letters but the elimination of two common failures: a task with nobody accountable, which drifts, and a task with three people accountable, which means nobody is. A map made at the start of a project prevents both.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step mapping exercise. First, the work is broken into tasks small enough that one person can be accountable for each. Second, each task is assigned exactly one accountable person, the person who answers if the task fails. Third, responsible people, the ones doing the work, are named, and consulted people are named only where their input genuinely changes the result. Fourth, the map is reviewed whenever the team or the scope changes, because a map that no longer matches reality is worse than no map, since it misleads. The map is shared where the work is tracked, not filed in a document nobody opens.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for responsibility mapping. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: launch page -> OK; support rota -> accountable must be exactly one Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when a project involves several people or teams and ownership is unclear. Do not use it to assign accountability to someone without the authority or time to carry it, because that only formalizes an overload. Do not use it as a performance tool, because its purpose is clarity about work, not judgment about people. title: Cross-Team Request Intake
body:
Cross-team request intake is the front door through which one team asks another team for work. Without a front door, requests arrive by hallway chat, private message, and forwarded email, and the receiving team cannot prioritize, because it cannot see the whole queue. With a front door, every request carries the same fields: what is wanted, why it matters, when it is needed, and what happens if it waits. The receiving team can then triage honestly, and the requesting team can see where its request stands instead of chasing individuals.

Method. The working method for this record is a six-field intake form plus a triage rhythm. First, the request states the outcome wanted, not just the task imagined, so the receiving team can propose a better way. Second, the requester states the deadline and the reason for it, distinguishing a real external deadline from a preferred date. Third, the requester states the impact of waiting, so triage has something to weigh. Fourth, the receiving team acknowledges every request within an agreed window, even if only to say it is queued. Fifth, triage happens on a visible schedule, and the queue order is visible to requesters. Sixth, requests that are declined are declined with a reason and an alternative, not left unanswered.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for cross-team request intake. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: priority 1 - fix login bug; priority 2 - update docs; priority 3 - new report Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record whenever two teams depend on each other's work on a recurring basis. Do not use it for emergencies, where direct contact and an agreed escalation path are the right tools. Do not use it to build a wall around a team, because intake that never says yes is a refusal system, not a collaboration system. title: Review as Collaboration
body:
Review as collaboration means treating review, of a document, a design, or a piece of work, as a joint improvement step rather than a gate where one person judges another. Good review finds real problems early, spreads knowledge about the work across the team, and leaves the author better equipped next time. Bad review becomes a bottleneck, a style argument, or a rubber stamp. The difference is mostly process: small review units, clear review criteria, timely turnaround, and comments that explain the concern and suggest a fix instead of merely pointing at a flaw.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part review practice. First, work is submitted in small pieces, because a large submission gets skimmed while a small one gets read. Second, the author states what kind of review is wanted, such as correctness, clarity, or completeness, so reviewers spend effort where it matters. Third, reviewers comment on the work with reasons and, where possible, suggested wording or fixes. Fourth, the author responds to each comment, either by changing the work or by explaining why not, so nothing is silently dropped. Fifth, turnaround is tracked, and a review that waits longer than the agreed window is escalated, because a queue of unreviewed work is a queue of blocked teammates.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for review as collaboration. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: reviews: 5 average turnaround days: 2.0; slowest: 4 fastest: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any work product that benefits from a second pair of eyes, from plans to published pages. Do not use it as a substitute for testing or checking against requirements, because review catches judgment errors, not every defect. Do not use it to slow urgent fixes, because emergency work needs a lighter, faster review path agreed in advance. title: Knowledge Sharing Systems
body:
A knowledge sharing system is the team's way of making what one person knows available to everyone who will need it later. The most common form is an internal wiki or shared guide collection, but the system is the habit, not the tool: writing things down when they are learned, keeping them current, and pointing people at them instead of answering the same question privately for the tenth time. Teams that share knowledge well onboard faster, survive absences better, and stop depending on a single expert for routine questions.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part sharing loop. First, when someone answers a question that others will ask again, the answer is written into the shared collection, not left in a private message. Second, each page names its owner and its last update date, so staleness is visible and fixable. Third, new joiners are pointed at the collection on day one and asked to note what is missing or confusing, because fresh eyes find gaps fastest. Fourth, the collection is pruned on a schedule: outdated pages are updated or archived, so search keeps returning live answers. A page's freshness is checked by age, and anything older than the team's agreed horizon is flagged for review.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for knowledge sharing systems. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: onboarding guide -> fresh (12 days old); server runbook -> STALE - review needed (210 days old); holiday policy -> fresh (45 days old); old launch plan -> STALE - review needed (400 days old) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any team whose knowledge lives mostly in people's heads. Do not use it as a dumping ground for every message, because an uncurated pile is as hard to search as no collection at all. Do not use it to replace mentoring, because some knowledge transfers only through working alongside someone. title: Team Onboarding Practice
body:
Team onboarding practice is the structured way a team brings a new member from first day to full contributor. Good onboarding is a collaboration act: the team prepares access, a first task, a buddy, and a map of where things live, before the person arrives. Poor onboarding leaves the newcomer to discover everything by asking, which taxes the whole team and slows the newcomer for weeks. The goal is not to flood the first week with documents but to sequence small, real contributions with support, so confidence and competence grow together.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part onboarding sequence. First, access and accounts are ready on day one, so the newcomer is not blocked by paperwork. Second, a buddy is named, a teammate whose job is to answer the questions a newcomer is embarrassed to ask twice. Third, the first task is small, real, and shippable within the first week, so the newcomer learns the team's workflow by doing it. Fourth, a guided tour of the team's documents, decisions, and current work happens in the first fortnight, with the newcomer noting gaps. Fifth, a check-in at thirty days reviews progress and adjusts the plan, because onboarding that is never reviewed drifts into neglect.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for team onboarding practice. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: onboarding progress: 3 of 5 steps; remaining: ['first task shipped', '30-day check-in'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for every joiner, including internal transfers, who face the same discovery burden as external hires. Do not use it as a substitute for role training or professional qualifications, which onboarding complements but does not replace. Do not use it to measure a newcomer against a fixed speed, because people arrive with different backgrounds and the plan should flex. title: Retrospectives and Feedback Loops
body:
A retrospective is a team's regular, structured look back at a period of work to decide what to keep, what to change, and what to try next. The format matters less than the loop: observations are gathered from everyone, patterns are named, a small number of actions are chosen with owners, and the next retrospective checks whether those actions happened. Without the loop, a retrospective is a venting session that changes nothing. With it, the team improves in small, visible steps, and people keep participating because they see their input turn into action.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step retrospective loop. First, data is gathered: what shipped, what slipped, and what surprised the team, from records rather than memory alone. Second, everyone contributes observations, including quieter members, in writing before discussion, so the loudest voice does not set the agenda. Third, the team groups observations into themes and picks at most three actions, because ten actions mean none get done. Fourth, each action gets an owner and a check date, and is tracked like any other work. Fifth, the next retrospective opens by reviewing the previous actions, closing the loop visibly.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for retrospectives and feedback loops. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: Ana owns 2 action(s); Ben owns 1 action(s) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any team that repeats work in cycles, from weekly delivery to quarterly planning. Do not use it to assign blame for failures, because a retrospective that punishes honesty stops receiving honest input. Do not use it as a status meeting, because its purpose is learning and change, not reporting. title: Facilitation to Agreement
body:
Facilitation to agreement is the skill of running a group discussion so it ends with a decision everyone can live with, rather than with the loudest opinion winning or the meeting ending without a call. A facilitator separates the roles of contributing ideas and managing the conversation, keeps the discussion on the question at hand, surfaces disagreement early while it is still cheap to resolve, and records the decision and its reasons before the group disperses. The technique is most valuable when the stakes are real and the group disagrees honestly.

Method. The working method for this record is a six-step facilitated discussion. First, the question to be decided is written down and agreed, so the group does not solve three different problems at once. Second, options are gathered before evaluation, so early judgment does not kill good ideas. Third, each option is scored against agreed criteria, in writing, so the comparison is visible rather than impressionistic. Fourth, disagreement is invited explicitly, with the facilitator asking who sees it differently and why. Fifth, the group chooses, and the choice is stated with its trade-offs, not as a false consensus. Sixth, the decision, its reasons, and its review trigger are logged, so the group does not reopen it without new information.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for facilitation to agreement. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: options scored: {'keep tool A': 7, 'adopt tool B': 9, 'build in-house': 4}; winner: adopt tool B with 9 points Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for decisions where several reasonable people disagree and the outcome must hold. Do not use it for decisions one person is accountable for, where consultation is right but group agreement is not required. Do not use it to manufacture agreement where real disagreement remains, because a forced consensus collapses at the first difficulty. title: Time-Zone Overlap Planning
body:
Time-zone overlap planning is how a distributed team arranges its shared hours so collaboration happens without forcing anyone into unreasonable hours. The team maps each member's working window onto a common clock, finds the overlap, and protects it for the conversations that truly need everyone present. Everything else moves to written async channels. Done well, overlap planning turns time zones from a daily friction into a relay: work passes westward as each region's day ends, and the overlap hours are spent on decisions, not status updates.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step overlap plan. First, every member's working window is recorded in a common reference, with local start and end times converted honestly, including any daylight changes the team must track. Second, the pairwise and whole-team overlaps are computed, so the team knows exactly how many shared hours exist rather than guessing. Third, the overlap is reserved for decision meetings, reviews, and unblocking, while status moves to writing. Fourth, the plan is revisited when membership or seasons change, because an overlap that quietly shrinks leaves teammates stranded in meetings at midnight. A small calculator that converts local windows to a shared clock makes the arithmetic reliable.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for time-zone overlap planning. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: UTC windows: [('London', 9, 17), ('New York', 14, 22), ('Berlin', 8, 16)]; whole-team overlap: 14:00 to 16:00 UTC (2 hours) Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any team spread across more than two time zones, or where meeting times keep drifting into someone's night. Do not use it to justify always scheduling at the majority's convenience, because the burden of awkward hours should rotate or be shared. Do not use it where the team can simply work async, because no overlap is needed when writing carries the work. title: Shared Ownership of Work
body:
Shared ownership is the arrangement where a team, not an individual, owns a service, a project, or a body of work, so knowledge, responsibility, and on-call load are spread rather than concentrated. Single ownership feels efficient until the owner is absent, overloaded, or leaves, at which point the work stalls and the team discovers how much lived in one head. Shared ownership costs coordination, because more people must stay current, but it buys resilience: any member can answer, fix, or hand over the work, and improvements come from several viewpoints instead of one.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part ownership system. First, the owned thing is named and its boundaries are written down, so ownership is of something definite. Second, at least two people are current on every critical part, so absence never blocks the work. Third, a rotation spreads recurring load, such as support duty, visibly and fairly, with swaps allowed but recorded. Fourth, changes are reviewed by someone other than the author, so knowledge spreads through review itself. Fifth, ownership is reviewed when the team changes, because an ownership map that still names departed members is a map of a team that no longer exists. A rotation schedule computed in advance makes fairness checkable rather than claimed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for shared ownership of work. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: week 1 duty: Ana; week 2 duty: Ben; week 3 duty: Cara; week 4 duty: Dan Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for services, systems, or projects the team must keep running over time. Do not use it where a single accountable decision-maker is required, because shared ownership of a decision can blur accountability; pair it with a responsibility map for decisions. Do not use it as a way to avoid naming anyone, because shared ownership still needs named people on the rotation. title: Collaborative Writing and Version Discipline
body:
Collaborative writing is how several people produce one document that reads as if one mind wrote it. The failure mode is familiar: sections in different voices, contradictory facts, and a final merge that silently drops someone's contribution. The discipline that prevents it is simple but strict: one outline agreed before drafting, one owner for the final voice, sections drafted in parallel against the outline, and a merge step that reviews the whole document for consistency rather than merely concatenating parts. Version discipline supports this by making clear which draft is current and what changed between drafts.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step collaborative writing process. First, the outline is agreed by all contributors, including the document's purpose, audience, and length, before any drafting starts. Second, sections are assigned with owners and deadlines, and each section states its key facts up front so contradictions surface early. Third, drafts are written in the shared document, not in private copies that must later be merged by hand. Fourth, one editor reads the assembled draft end to end for voice, consistency, and gaps, and returns it for fixes. Fifth, versions are dated and summarized, so a reader can tell what changed and why, and the published version is frozen while a new draft begins.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for collaborative writing and version discipline. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: unique contributions: 3 [('Ana', 'intro'), ('Ben', 'methods'), ('Cara', 'results')] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for reports, guides, and proposals written by more than one person. Do not use it for creative writing where a single voice is the point, or for legal documents where formal review and approval processes govern. Do not use it to let the loudest contributor overwrite others silently, because the merge step exists to protect every contribution. title: Blameless Joint Problem Solving
body:
Blameless joint problem solving is a team's way of learning from failures without turning the review into a trial. When something goes wrong, the team reconstructs the timeline, names the contributing conditions, and fixes the system, rather than hunting for a person to blame. The reason is practical, not soft: people who expect blame hide mistakes, so the team learns nothing and the same failure repeats. People who expect a fair review report problems early, when they are cheap to fix, and the team's systems get steadily harder to break.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step blameless review. First, a timeline is built from records, not memory, showing what happened in order. Second, contributing conditions are named, including confusing tooling, missing checks, unclear ownership, and time pressure, alongside any human error. Third, the team asks what a reasonable, well-intentioned person would have done with the same information, which separates system flaws from individual fault. Fourth, actions are chosen that change the system, such as adding a check, clarifying ownership, or fixing a confusing interface, rather than actions that merely tell people to be more careful. Fifth, the review and its actions are shared with the wider team, so the learning spreads beyond the people in the room.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for blameless joint problem solving. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 09:00 - deploy started; 09:12 - alert fired; 09:20 - rollback begun; 09:35 - service restored; events recorded: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record after any failure, outage, or near miss where the team wants the same thing not to happen again. Do not use it to excuse genuine misconduct, which belongs in a separate process, because conflating the two corrupts both. Do not use it as a report that nobody reads, because a review without tracked actions is theater. title: Team Working Agreements
body:
A team working agreement is a short, written, team-authored set of promises about how the team will work together: how it communicates, how it decides, how it handles disagreement, and how it treats each other's time. Unlike a policy imposed from above, an agreement the team writes itself is one the team will actually defend, because everyone had a hand in it. The agreement is revisited regularly, because a team that grows or changes its work needs its promises to change too. The document itself is short; its value is in the conversation that produces it and the shared reference it leaves behind.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part agreement process. First, the team discusses its real frictions, not abstract values, and names the behaviors that help and the ones that hurt. Second, the team writes promises as observable behaviors, such as reply within one working day, rather than vague aspirations, such as be respectful. Third, the agreement is signed by the whole team and kept where the work happens, not filed away. Fourth, the team reviews the agreement at a fixed rhythm, such as quarterly, and updates it as the team changes. Fifth, breaches are raised kindly and early, against the agreement rather than against a person, so the agreement stays a living tool instead of a dead poster.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for team working agreements. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: promises kept: 3 of 4; to improve: ['no meeting without an agenda'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any team that wants its collaboration norms to be explicit instead of assumed. Do not use it as a disciplinary document, because an agreement enforced as a rulebook loses the consent that makes it work. Do not use it to freeze norms that should evolve, because the review rhythm is part of the agreement, not an optional extra.
